1: # Chalkboard — Style Prompt
2: 
3: > A real classroom blackboard on which chalk writes itself, stroke by stroke in true stroke order, with no hand, no chalk stick and no eraser in sight. One idea is taught the way a teacher does it: write what people think, wipe it with one pass, write what is true in the same place.
4: > References (grammar only): a primary-school literacy lesson on a sliding double blackboard; the way a teacher underlines the parts of a character, circles one component and wipes a wrong line. Take the order of a lesson, not any teacher's handwriting.
5: 
6: Suits short lessons on one idea: where a word or a character comes from, a misconception set right, a worked problem. The length follows how many steps the lesson has.
7: 
8: ## 1. Essence, and what it is not
9: 
10: - **A clean, freshly wiped board.** One even deep ink green with its own fine grain and very slow mottling. No history on the slate: no old swirls, no ghost lessons, no floating dust, no bokeh.
11: - **Writing that grows like a hand writes.** Strokes appear along their centre line in the correct stroke order, with pressure: pressed starts and corners, points that lift, 捺 feet that spread, hooks flicked off.
12: - **Three chalks at most.** White for structure, one accent chalk for the single part the lesson tracks, one pale chalk for a second hand (a pupil, a visitor).
13: - **A real object in a real room.** Wooden frame, a tray with sticks of chalk, painted tian-zi grids, sliding panels, a wall and a clock around it.
14: - **Few words, large letters.** The board holds keywords; the explanation is spoken.
15: 
16: Not Whiteboard Explainer: that style is a bright glossy board, coloured markers, floating marker props and magnets, ghost marks of old lessons, and a camera travelling across a knowledge map of many regions to explain how something works. Chalkboard is a dark matte slate with nothing floating in front of it, kept clean, one question per board, the camera facing it flat; it advances by writing a claim, wiping it and rewriting in place, and it lives in a classroom (panels that slide, grids painted on, a tray, a wall). Not a slide either: nothing is typeset, nothing fades in.
17: 
18: ## 2. Materials & rendering
19: 
20: - Canvas 2D for everything visible; WebGL2 only for the post pass (camera motion blur, a light vignette, grade, dither).
21: - Each stroke is baked once into a board-space coverage sprite (coverage, arc length, lateral position). A partial stroke reveals pixels up to the current arc length with a round leading edge; the board's grain decides which grains take the chalk (deposit with a 2×2 supersample and a faint powder halo).
22: - Chalk edges are firm; loose powder only at the lift-off of a stroke (two to five grains). Never sugar the board.
23: - Writing strokes carry a width profile per stroke type (start bump, corner bumps, taper for 撇 / 提, foot for 捺, quick lift for hooks) and a pressure profile (heavier at both ends, lighter in the middle). Straight strokes bow slightly; horizontals rise 2–3° to the right; 横, 竖 and 折 enter with a short pressed tick from the upper left.
24: - Board, panels, frame, tray, clock and wall are baked once in world units; the slate grain is a periodic tile drawn in world space (soft-light) only when the camera is close.
25: - Erasing is a blurred destination-out band along one smooth path on a layer that holds only the strokes being wiped; it leaves a very thin, even haze. One wipe per film is plenty.
26: - A wet streak (a board just wiped with a damp cloth) is a soft mask with a wide blur at its drying edge, fading at top and bottom, that darkens the slate slightly; never a hard rim.
27: - Light: a gentle multiply falloff away from the windows and at most a faint warm window patch. Light never draws shapes across the writing in close shots.
28: 
29: ## 3. Colour logic
30: 
31: - Ground: deep ink green slate, wood frame, warm white wall and a coloured dado if the room is seen.
32: - White chalk carries every structure: characters, lines, labels, arrows.
33: - The accent chalk (example: orange) is reserved for the one component the lesson tracks; it never decorates and never draws arrows or underlines that are not that component.
34: - A pale second chalk (example: yellow) marks another person's handwriting.
35: - No rainbow, no gradients in chalk, no glow. Painted grids are dull and thin so the chalk always wins.
36: 
37: ## 4. Type & subtitles
38: 
39: - Chinese is hand-authored stroke data (centre lines + stroke type per stroke) drawn by the chalk engine, never a font's outline. Every character the topic needs is added to the data and checked against an OFL kai font behind it before shooting (how: §10, *New characters*).
40: - English on the board is a single-line OFL handwriting font (EMS family) drawn by the same engine; symbols missing from the font (arrows, plus) are drawn as strokes.
41: - On the board: keywords only, one line of Chinese, the next line English, a size smaller.
42: - Sizes at 1080p: big characters 300–450 px; labels ≥ 55 px CJK and ≥ 30 px Latin cap height; small writing gets heavier chalk so no stroke is thinner than 3 px.

45: ### Voice and subtitles
46: 
47: - When the style tells a story it is narrated: one calm teacher's voice in short spoken sentences, said as the matching chalk appears; what the voice names is being written or shown at that moment.
48: - A quiet subtitle plate sits above the bottom safe area: the spoken line in Chinese and a free English translation, one line each, a plain kai face (an OFL subset) on a soft dark plate, in and out with the voice. Long lines are split at sentence ends into several cues.
49: - Nothing the viewer must read on the board sits behind the plate; frames held for the board's words are composed above it.
50: - Pauses between voice lines are short (0.25–0.4 s); one longer hold (about 1.5 s) is kept for the verdict. Board action (a panel sliding, a wipe) runs under the voice instead of waiting for it.

52: ## 5. Motion quality
53: 
54: - 30 fps, continuous (render with `--fps 30`: `core/render/video.mjs` defaults to 24).
55: - Chalk speed, measured on our demo: a big character takes about 0.1 s per stroke including the air between strokes (a ten-stroke character about 1 s), labels about 0.04 s per stroke. Writing speeds up rather than making the voice wait, but a big character written much faster than about 0.07 s per stroke stops looking like a hand.
56: - When reading time and chalk speed pinch in a short film, change the words, not the hand. Ways that work (choose per film): fewer and shorter blocks on the board; big characters only for what the lesson tracks, everything else at label size; start a block while the voice is still on the previous line, so it is finished when it is named; write the next block while the last one is still being read in the same frame; hold the frame instead of moving on; make the film longer.
57: - Camera eases in and out (cubic), never bounces except a whip landing.
58: - Things appear only by being written, wiped, revealed by a sliding panel or by drying. Nothing fades in.

60: ## 6. Camera grammar
61: 
62: The camera always faces the board flat on (no perspective tilt).
63: 
64: | Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
65: |---|---|---|
66: | Close shot on the writing | attention on how a character or line is built | a component; a step of a proof; a spelling |
67: | Slow lateral pan along a line | time or sequence | a timeline; a derivation; a list of cases |
68: | Pull back to a fixed medium frame | the whole question at once | a comparison; a claim and its counter-claim |
69: | Same frame later | judgement | a correction; a before / after |
70: | Locked frame while a panel slides | a page turned in the room's own way | a new chapter; a hidden board |
71: | Whip with motion blur (≤ 0.5 s) | a jump to another part of the wall | a change of board |
72: | Cut on a line crossing a seam | a connection | cause and effect; the same part in two places |
73: | Wide shot of the whole wall | summary | the map of what was learnt |
74: 
75: The room is part of the style: at least once the frame opens wide enough to read board, frame, tray and wall as a classroom (where, and what else the room holds, is the film's choice). Close shots may show only slate and frame.
76: 
77: Rules: the subject is never smaller than a third of the frame in close shots; text blocks are never cut by the frame edge while they are read; no empty board for more than half a second. Transitions are hard cuts, a sliding panel or a line across a seam; no dissolves or page flips.

79: ## 7. Sound palette
80: 
81: - Voice first: it is the loudest element; music sits 15–18 dB under it and comes up only in the pauses.
82: - Foley: real chalk recordings cut into grains, one grain chain per stroke, level from stroke size; a light knock on landings; the accent chalk slightly softer and duller. A felt pass for the wipe, the low roll of a sliding panel ending on a stop, room tone very low; school sounds (a distant bell) only as punctuation. Where the recordings come from and how to cut them: §10, *Sound*.
83: - Music: sparse plucked strings (a guqin model or nylon guitar) with marimba and pizzicato bass; a plucked note can be "born" from something drawn. Silence while a question or a verdict is read.
84: - Mix: about −16 LUFS integrated before mastering, true peak ≤ −1.5 dBFS.

86: ## 8. Native moves
87: 
88: - **Write, wipe, rewrite in place.** The wrong reading is written under its object, wiped with one pass, and the right one written in the same spot from the same camera position. *Fits content like:* a common misconception in physics; a misremembered date; a sum everybody gets wrong.
89: - **Tracked component in accent chalk.** One part keeps its colour and its height across several forms. *Fits content like:* a root through a word family; a variable through an equation's rearrangements; a gene through generations.
90: - **Sliding panel reveal.** The front panel slides away to show a clean back board, and can slide back to close the lesson. *Fits content like:* "but before that…"; the hidden proof; the answer kept back.
91: - **A line that sews two boards.** One accent line runs across the seam to join two places. *Fits content like:* the same constant in two formulas; a quote and its source; cause and effect.
92: - **Drying wet streak.** The freshly wiped board dries back and reveals what was left untouched. *Fits content like:* yesterday's question; a note left by a student; a reminder at the corner.
93: - **Second hand.** A different, childlike chalk colour and hand on the same board. *Fits content like:* a pupil's question; a visitor's comment; a wrong attempt.
94: - **Chalk as a measuring tool.** An accent object laid along a white line and ticked off, so a comparison is shown, not told. *Fits content like:* a unit's origin; a scale; how many of one thing fit another.

96: ## 9. Pitfalls of the medium
97: 
98: - Dirty boards (old swirls, ghosts, floating dust) read as "messy", not "real". Keep the slate clean and let the grain carry the realism.
99: - Equal-width polylines look like a plotter and make characters misread. Use stroke-type width and pressure profiles.
100: - Character data that is structurally wrong is caught at once by native readers: check every character against a reference before shooting.
101: - Small writing at 1080p disappears with the same chalk width as large writing; give small text heavier chalk.
102: - Text written while the camera moves away fails reading time; hold the frame or keep the block in view.
103: - Accent colour spread over arrows and decorations stops meaning anything.
104: - A soft halo at the chalk's front reads as glow. The demo's `drawFront` (`props.js`) puts a faint radial gradient under its grains: in your copy, drop the gradient and keep the grains.
105: - A wet streak with a hard edge looks like a cut-out.
106: - Board-speak in the voice ("A plus B", component names with no meaning) is not understood: every component is said with what it means the first time it appears.

108: ## 10. Engine
109: 
110: The demo's code is a working engine; copy it into the project folder and write the film yourself.
111: 
112: **Copy as is:** `js/chalk.js` (`Stroke`, `bake`, `drawStroke`: the chalk), `js/hand.js` (`writeChar(ch, cx, cy, size, clock, o)`, `writeLine` for mixed Chinese and Latin, `writeLatin`, `latinWidth`, `loadSvgFont`; each returns `Stroke[]` with `t0`/`t1` set and `.end` = the time the last stroke ends), `js/r2d.js` (grain tile, deposit), `js/stage.js` (slates, frame, tray, clock, wall, `paintGrid`; world units: slate x 0…6400, y 0…1700, panel width `PW` 3200), `js/post.js`, `js/lab.js`, `tools/foley_lib.py`, `tools/subset.py` (subtitle font cut from the strings in `SUB` in `film.js`), `tools/srt.py`. `js/props.js` too, minus the glow (§9).
113: 
114: **Adapt:** `js/hz.js` (keep its characters, add yours), `index.html` (title), `js/app.js` (the compositor: it draws the layers, wet streak, wipe, light, subtitle plate and exposes `render`, `TEXTS`, `DUR`, `EV`; edit it to the film's board instead of feeding it placeholder data).
115: 
116: **Write yourself:** `js/film.js` (every stroke, time, camera key, voice start and subtitle, as data), the voice lines, the score and mix (`audio.py` is the demo's own score; its chalk-grain part is reusable), `build.sh`. `js/ancient.js` is the demo's old forms of one character: not an engine file.
117: 
118: **What `app.js` reads from `build(W, H)` in `film.js`:**
119: 
120: | Field | What it is |
121: |---|---|
122: | `S` | every `Stroke`, each with `layer`: `'FL'` (the sliding front panel, in panel-local units, moved by `slideX`), `'FR'` (the right panel, world units), `'BK'` (the back board, drawn only once the panel has moved), `'WORLD'` (on top, world units, drawn while `t < T.back0`); FL strokes also carry `phase` (`'pre'` = can be wiped, `wiped: true` = removed by the wipe; `'post'` = written after it). `o.R` sets bake resolution (default 2) |
123: | `DUR` | length in seconds |
124: | `camAt(t)` | `{cx, cy, s, shot}`: centre in world units, scale for a 1920-wide frame, shot index (motion blur is only taken within one shot) |
125: | `slideX(t)` | the front panel's offset; `() => 0` if it never moves |
126: | `TX` | board text for readcheck: `{id, text, layer, box:[x0,y0,x1,y1] in that layer's units, t0, t1}` |
127: | `SUBS` | subtitle cues `{id, t0, t1, zh, en}` |
128: | `EV` | sound events for `core/render/events.mjs`: `vo` (voice starts), `sub` (for the .srt), `chalk` (`t, d, len, color, pan, big`, one per stroke) and any of your own |
129: | `G1`, `G2`, `SMALL`, `T.back0`, `wet`, `wipe` | painted grids on the front panel and back board; when the closing slide starts; the wet streak `{x0, y0, y1, xEnd, bx0, t0, t1}`; the wipe `{t0, t1, w, path}` |
130: 
131: A film without a wet streak, a wipe, grids or a sliding panel removes those parts from its copy of `app.js` (or guards them, e.g. `if (!F.wet) return` at the top of `drawWet`, `if (!F.wipe) return null` in `drawWipeHaze`), and draws `WORLD` strokes on a condition of its own if there is no closing slide. Don't pass dummy fields to keep the compositor quiet.
132: 
133: **New characters.** `hz.js` maps a character to its strokes in standard stroke order (GF 0023-2020); each stroke is `"type x,y x,y …"`: the centre line through its anchor points in a 100 × 100 box, y down. Types: `h` 横, `s` 竖, `p` 撇, `n` 捺, `d` 点, `t` 提, `x` 悬针竖; `z…` for turns (corners pressed); a last letter `g` ends in a hook (its last point is the hook's tip), `p` / `t` in a point, `d` in a dot. Write only the centre line: the slight bow, the rise of horizontals and the pressed entry tick are added by `writeChar`. Symbols (arrows, plus, a tick) are written the same way. A way that works:
134: 
135: 1. Take the stroke order and count from a dictionary that shows the standard order, and write down the type sequence first.
136: 2. Set the character large from the reference kai (LXGW WenKai, `fonts/`) on a 100-unit grid, placed as the check page places it so the numbers line up: e.g. with PIL, `ImageFont.truetype(font, 1000)` drawn into a 1000 × 1000 image at `(0, 880)` with `anchor='ls'` (left edge, baseline at 0.88 of the box), with 100-px grid lines; read each stroke's start, corners and end off it and divide by 10. Keep the anchors on the middle of the font's stroke, not its edge.
137: 3. Open `index.html?lab=hz&chars=<new characters>&size=400`: the chalk is drawn over the font in red. Check stroke count and order, which strokes touch or cross and which stop short, the proportion of each component, hook directions and the 撇/捺 feet; then look again at the size the film uses for it. Fix the numbers, not the font.
138: 4. Read it at film size the way a native reader would, before shooting (§9): a structure that looks right at 400 px over the font can still read as another character on its own.
139: 
140: **Sound.** Three CC0 / CC BY recordings of chalk on a board from Wikimedia Commons (URLs in the demo's `build.sh`, credits in `CREDITS`) are cut into tagged grains with `python -I tools/foley_lib.py <out_dir> <name>=<file> …`: `tap`, `stroke` and `squeak` grains plus `index.json` with each grain's length, attack and brightness. The demo's `audio.py` places one grain chain per `chalk` event (length from `d`, level from `len`, the accent chalk low-passed); other recordings can be cut the same way.
141: 
142: **Render.** `node core/render/events.mjs <film>` (events from the page), your mix, `node core/render/video.mjs <film> --fps 30`, `sh core/render/mux.sh <video> <mix> <out> 30 1`, `node core/render/readcheck.mjs <film>`. The page bakes every stroke on load (about 10 s for 500 strokes), then 20–50 ms per 1080p frame. readcheck counts from the first frame a block's box is on screen, which is when its writing starts: leave the reading time after the last stroke yourself (§4).

1: # Directing a Lemo-Opuscar film
2: 
3: The directing method behind every film in this library. Pair it with one `styles/<slug>/STYLE.md` (the style) and [`TECHNIQUE.md`](TECHNIQUE.md) (how to build).
4: 
5: You are the director, not a tech demo. A film is judged in this order: **sound, rhythm, camera, directing** (performance, staging, emotional arc). Good-looking frames are only the starting point.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 1. Take the brief
10: 
11: The user gives a style and a topic, sometimes more (length, language, voice, must-have shots, brand rules). Everything else is your decision. Ask once, in a single message (AGENTS.md, Workflow), then no more questions. Defaults:
12: 
13: - Length **30–60 s**; shorter and tight beats padded. Beyond two or three minutes multiplies time and token cost: tell the user.
14: - 1920×1080 at 24 fps by default; an output frame rate set in the style's `STYLE.md` (30 or 60 fps, for example) wins, and is what you pass to `--fps` and `mux.sh`; other sizes (vertical 1080×1920, for example) with `--size WxH` on the render tools.
15: - Voice and subtitles in the language the user writes in. Subtitles burned in and exported as `.srt`.
16: - Loudness −14 LUFS.
17: 
18: Say it in the questions when it matters: a good Chinese voice uses Microsoft's online service (edge-tts) and needs a connection; offline, Kokoro reads Chinese but sounds plain (TECHNIQUE.md §4).
19: 
20: Requests that only change the plan:
21: 
22: - **No voice, or no subtitles.** Drop those steps and say so in the treatment.
23: - **Their own voice recording.** Use it as it is; transcribe it with faster-whisper for word timings.
24: - **Their own material**: logos, photos, footage, and for styles built from real material (the Evidence Films) their own data, scans, imagery or CAD. Ask whether they have any; what they give comes first, and the sources in the `STYLE.md` are the fallback. Before you download from those sources, tell the user what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. Rights: section 12.
25: 
26: ## 2. Find a benchmark first
27: 
28: Before writing anything, pick one or two reference works (films, title sequences, games, ads) that set the bar for this style **and this topic**. They are your choice, made for the user's film; don't borrow the demo's. Write down:
29: 
30: - **What to learn**: composition, pacing, camera grammar, colour logic, score structure.
31: - **What not to take**: characters, designs, melodies, specific shots, logos, fonts.
32: 
33: The benchmark lifts quality more than any rule below.
34: 
35: ## 3. Shape the story
36: 
37: - **One subject, one goal, one turn.** A character (or a single object, product or idea) wants something, something changes, it ends differently from how it began.
38: - **Hook in the first 3 seconds.** No slow logo reveal before anything happens.
39: - **An ending that echoes.** Bookend the opening, reveal the scale, or let the character do the thing right the second time.
40: - **One native move**: a moment only this medium can do (a fold that becomes a transition, ink that blooms into the next scene, a type grid that snaps into the logo). Put it at the emotional peak. `STYLE.md` lists the medium's native moves; pick or invent the one your story needs.
41: - **Cut the extras.** One gag the audience reads at thumbnail size beats three they can't. If a beat needs explaining, remove it.
42: 
43: ## 4. Write the treatment
44: 
45: Write `TREATMENT.md` before drawing anything, and before you open the style's `DEMO.md` or demo code (an Edit & Documentary style gathers its material first: AGENTS.md, "Treatment first"):
46: 
47: 1. **Three candidate structures**, a few lines each (for example: a single journey, a before/after, a countdown, a list that turns), then the one you chose and why. Choose the opening image, the ending and the shape of the score from the topic too; the first idea that comes to mind for a style is usually its cliché.
48: 2. **Logline and arc**: one sentence, then setup → turn → ending.
49: 3. **Benchmark**: learn / don't learn (section 2).
50: 4. **Shot list**: for every shot, the framing (wide / full / medium / close / insert), angle, camera move (push, pull, pan, track, crane, zoom), duration, and **why** it is shot that way.
51: 5. **Beat sheet**, second by second.
52: 6. **Cue map**: tempo, bar grid, instrumentation per section, and on which beat every cut, key action and subtitle lands.
53: 7. **Sound design table**: for each section, the ambience bed, the main foley and the music state.
54: 8. **Subtitle and title design**: the type is part of the style.
55: 
56: ## 5. Prove the look
57: 
58: - **With characters**: draw a model sheet (turnaround, 3–4 expressions, 2–3 key poses, palette) plus two style frames.
59: - **Without characters**: three style frames from the film, one of them the signature shot.
60: 
61: Render them with the real drawing code, not a mock-up, and check them yourself against the `STYLE.md` before going on.
62: 
63: ### The storyboard (only if the user asked for one)
64: 
65: Render 6–9 key shots with the real drawing code, tiled into one sheet (`core/render/sheet.py`) with shot number, framing, duration and line under each. Send it with the logline and what you are least sure about, and **wait for approval**. If the user didn't ask for one, don't stop.
66: 
67: ## 6. Sound is half the film
68: 
69: - **Every visible action has a sound**: landings, page turns, cuts, drips, clicks, cloth. Match the material (paper, wood, metal, ink and glass all sound different).
70: - **Three layers**: ambience (room, wind, rain, city), foley (tied to actions) and music. Duck the music under dialogue and key foley.
71: - **At least two real silences**, or near-silences, before the turn or the emotional peak. The first sound after the silence should be one of the most important sounds in the film.
72: - **Use sound as a transition** at least twice: bring the next scene's sound in early (J-cut) or let the last scene's sound run over the cut (L-cut).
73: - **Avoid generic "piano and strings".** Score in the instruments of the style's sound palette.
74: 
75: ## 7. Rhythm: the music grid comes first
76: 
77: - Write the cue map before animating. The picture locks to the grid, and a script checks every cue (TECHNIQUE.md §3).
78: - **Vary the pace**: alternate fast and slow, include one clear acceleration or deceleration, and give the audience one breath (a long take or a held pause). A film at one even speed has failed.
79: - One action, one sound, one cut, but don't cut on every beat. Leave time to see.
80: - **Pace for the viewer, not the clock**:
81:   - Hold every subtitle at least 1.8 s, and never shorter than the spoken line + 0.6 s.
82:   - After text finishes animating in, hold it for roughly (letters ÷ 15 + 1.5) s in English, (characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5) s in Chinese; `readcheck.mjs` checks this for you.
83:   - Hold a title card at least 4 s.
84:   - Give failures and gags enough time to be understood.
85:   - Fast is fine; make it fast with fewer words per screen, not by cutting before people finish reading.
86: 
87: ## 8. Camera: every shot needs a reason
88: 
89: - Use at least **four different camera moves** and real changes of framing. 2D has a camera too: push, pull, parallax, focus pulls, frames within frames.
90: - **One signature shot** people remember: a oner, a scale reveal, a transition made from the medium itself.
91: - **Design transitions inside the medium** (a page turn, a carved line growing, ink spreading), as one consistent grammar. Avoid default fades and hard cuts.
92: - At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height, with clear staging and a readable silhouette.
93: 
94: ## 9. Performance
95: 
96: - **Anticipation, action, follow-through** on every meaningful move. Characters change emotion. They do not just slide across the screen.
97: - **Motion continuity**, especially for characters built from code rigs:
98:   - Blend every pose with keyframes and easing; never switch poses inside an `if`. The only exception is a deliberate one-frame comic pop.
99:   - Check shoulders and arms on a large action test sheet (reach, raise, run, kneel) before shooting (TECHNIQUE.md §10).
100:   - Held props sit **between the palms**, at a depth between the two arms. A hand-over interpolates from one palm to the other. A rolling object turns by distance ÷ radius.
101:   - Step through key actions at 0.2 s intervals, enlarged.
102: - Check every expression at final size, especially eyebrow direction: "worried" and "angry" are one flip apart.
103: 
104: ## 10. The failures we saw most
105: 
106: - Subject too small, too far away, or pushed against the frame edge.
107: - Too dark to read, or a colour laid on the same colour (red on red).
108: - Subtitles covering the subject.
109: - A gag or failure too fast to understand.
110: - Blank frames in transitions.
111: - A timed effect (iris, zoom, follow cam) that doesn't track the subject after the camera moves (one world → screen function, TECHNIQUE.md §2).
112:

114: 
115: - Run the review loop (TECHNIQUE.md §8): contact sheets, 0.2 s strips of key actions, one full-speed viewing with sound.
116: - **One fix round.** Fix everything the review and the checks below find in one round, then check once more. Small fixes that second check turns up (a level, a frame) belong to the same round; anything bigger, tell the user in one line when you deliver. The user's notes after delivery are new rounds: change only what they ask.
117: - **Not the demo again.** After the treatment, read `DEMO.md` and compare: structure, opening, signature shot, camera path, score shape, ending. 118: - Voice: every line transcribes back correctly (speech-to-text check). For Chinese, one misheard character in a short line is normal: listen, and if it is right, let the check expect what the model heard (TECHNIQUE.md §4).

120: - Every row of the sound design table is actually in the mix.
121: - Every map, globe or satellite view passes section 13, checked enlarged.

3: Every film here is made from code: no video generation, no stock footage. This page explains the pipeline, to reproduce with our tools in `core/` or in your own stack. Pair it with [`DIRECTOR.md`](DIRECTOR.md) and one `styles/<slug>/STYLE.md`. Every command and flag is in [`core/README.md`](core/README.md).
4: 
5: ```
6: timeline (single source of truth)
7:    ├─► picture:  web page with render(t) ──► headless Chrome, frame by frame ──► video.mp4
8:    ├─► voice:    TTS per line ──► speech-to-text check ──► word timings
9:    ├─► music:    score from the same timeline (samples + synthesis) ──► stems
10:    ├─► sound:    procedural foley at event times
11:    └─► subtitles: .srt + burned-in captions
12: mix (duck, compress, balance) ──► mux with ffmpeg, two-pass loudnorm −14 LUFS ──► film.mp4
13: ```

15: ## 1. Requirements and install
16: 
17: System tools, which the user installs: **Node 20+**, **ffmpeg 7+** (6.x under-reports audio length through `loudnorm`, and `mux.sh` then rejects the file as cut off), and **Python 3.11+** or [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Developed on macOS (Apple silicon); Linux should work; on Windows use WSL. 3D and shader-heavy styles want a GPU.
18: 
19: Everything else installs in tiers, from the library root (`$LIB` in skill mode). Install a tier only when the film needs it:
20: 
21: | Command | Adds | Size |
22: |---|---|---|
23: | `sh plugin/skills/lemo-opuscar/scripts/setup.sh deps` | core: npm packages, headless browser, Python `.venv` (numpy, scipy, soundfile, soxr, pillow): render, synthesize sound, mux | ~350 MB |
24: | `… setup.sh deps voice` | Kokoro + model (English, offline), edge-tts (Chinese, online), faster-whisper (voice check) | ~0.55 GB + a Whisper model on first check (~145 MB for English, ~480 MB for Chinese) |
25: | `… setup.sh deps music` | numba, for plucked strings (`pluck.py`); the sampler itself needs only the core | ~140 MB |
26: | `sh tools/fetch.sh instruments <lib>` | a sample library: `freepats`, `karoryfer`, `salamander`, `vcsl`, `vsco2ce` or `all` | 70–400 MB each |
27: | `sh tools/fetch.sh hdri` | HDRIs for 3D styles | 12 MB |

29: Some styles need packages of their own (a LiDAR reader, a slide-scan decoder, a CAD importer); the style's `STYLE.md` lists them. They are packages, not system tools: install them yourself into a private venv or `node_modules` in the project folder, never into `$LIB/.venv`.

31: A synthesized score needs no big download; `sampler.py` names the library to fetch when an instrument is missing. A pack needs about twice its size free while it unpacks. Downloads come from npm, PyPI, GitHub Releases and Hugging Face (`HF_ENDPOINT` sets a mirror).

33: ## 2. The picture is a function of time
34: 
35: Each film is a folder with an `index.html` (`<demo>` in the commands) that exposes:
36: 
37: ```js
38: window.DUR = 54.2;                 // seconds
39: window.render = (t) => { ... };    // draw the frame at time t, deterministic
40: window.READY = true;               // set once fonts and images are loaded
41: window.EV = [{t, type, ...}];      // optional: sound / cue events for the mixer
42: window.TEXTS = (t) => [{id, text, x0, y0, x1, y1}];   // optional: every text visible at t, for readcheck
43: ```
44: 
45: **Paths:** pages reach library files with absolute URLs (`/core/lib.js`, `/node_modules/three/build/three.module.js`); scripts and `build.sh` use `$LIB`. Never `../..`.
46: 
47: A `build.sh` that works in both modes (in skill mode, put `LIB=<path setup.sh printed>` at the top):
48: 
49: ```sh
50: #!/bin/sh
51: set -e
52: HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
53: LIB=${LIB:-$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)}          # clone mode: <repo>/films/<name>/
54: export LIB
55: [ -f "$LIB/core/render/video.mjs" ] || { echo "set LIB to the library folder"; exit 1; }
56: cd "$LIB"
57: node core/render/events.mjs "$HERE"
58: node core/render/video.mjs "$HERE" --fps 24 --out "$HERE/out/video.mp4"
59: "$LIB/.venv/bin/python" "$HERE/mix.py"                               # score, foley, voice → out/mix.wav
60: sh core/render/mux.sh "$HERE/out/video.mp4" "$HERE/out/mix.wav" "$HERE/<name>.mp4" 24
61: ```
62: 
63: Rules that keep it reliable:
64: 
65: - **Deterministic.** No `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()` without a seed (`core/lib.js` has `mulberry` and `hash`), no state carried from the previous frame. Any frame can be rendered alone, in any order, by any worker.
66: - **Canvas 2D** for most 2D styles; **three.js** for 3D (§9); **WebGL2** shaders for post passes (film damage, CRT, ink redraw).
67: - **Animate on twos where the style wants it** (12 fps stepping for stop-motion, pixel or cel looks), but keep the camera and light smooth every frame. A stepped camera reads as lag.
68: - **One world → screen function.** Any effect that follows a subject (iris, zoom, spotlight) goes through it. Never hand-type screen coordinates.
69: - **Draw for the frame you render.** The default is 1920×1080; for another size pass `--size WxH` (e.g. `1080x1920`) to every render tool and lay the page out from `innerWidth` × `innerHeight`.
70: 
71: Capture (`core/render/`):
72: 
73: ```sh
74: node core/render/still.mjs <demo> 1.5 12 --range 0:50:2   # review stills; exits on page errors
75: node core/render/video.mjs <demo> --fps 24 --workers 3     # all frames → <demo>/out/video.mp4
76: node core/render/events.mjs <demo>                         # export DUR + EV → events.json
77: node core/render/readcheck.mjs <demo>                      # every on-screen text stays long enough to read
78: ```
79: 
80: To render a second version with other content, pass it to the page and give it its own output: `--q 'content=content_alt.json' --out …/alt.mp4` (the same for `events.mjs`).
81: 
82: Capture is fast because of **JPEG screenshots**, **one browser per worker** and **grain added in ffmpeg**: grain drawn in the page makes every frame incompressible and slow.
83: 
84: ## 3. One timeline drives everything
85: 
86: Keep sections, tempo, beats and hit points in one file (`timeline.js`). Export it to JSON and let the score, the mixer, the subtitles and the checks read the same numbers:
87: 
88: ```js
89: export const SECS = [{ id: 'chase', t: 12.0, bpm: 144, beats: 12 }, ...];
90: export const HIT  = { pratfall: ['chase', 6], ... };   // section + beat
91: ```
92: 
93: A small script (`cuecheck.py`, in `styles/<slug>/demo/tools/` of several demos) compares every visual hit with the music cue it should land on. Aim for 0 ms.
94: 
95: ## 4. Voice
96: 
97: - **TTS is only the default.** If the user brings a recording or names a voice, use that. Otherwise:
98:   - **English**: [Kokoro](https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx), local, many voices (an unknown `voice` name makes `tts.py` print the full list; `af_` / `am_` are American, `bf_` / `bm_` British; cast the narrator for this film, not the demo's). `core/tts/tts.py lines.json out/` writes one WAV per line and a durations file. Its Chinese voices (`"lang": "cmn"`) work offline but sound plain.
99:   - **Chinese**: `core/tts/tts_zh.py lines.json out/` uses [edge-tts](https://github.com/rany2/edge-tts) with Microsoft's neural voices (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`, `zh-CN-YunxiNeural`…), with the same outputs as `tts.py`, a rate per line and the silence trimmed. **It needs a network connection.**
100: - Spell numbers out in the TTS text and write them as digits in the subtitles.
101: - **Check every line**: `core/tts/asr_check.py` transcribes each WAV with faster-whisper and compares it with the script (`--lang zh`: numbers by value, so 十九 matches 19, and the rest character by character); re-generate until it exits 0. A misheard character in a short Chinese line is normal: listen, and if it is right, put what the model heard in the line's `asr` field. It also writes word timestamps for placing lines and subtitles.
102: - **Before mixing**: TTS has a high peak-to-average ratio. Compress the voice first, then balance by RMS: voice about 10 dB above the music.
103: 
104: ## 5. Music
105: 
106: Write an original score from the cue map, in the instruments of the style's sound palette; no generic piano and strings.
107: 
108: - **Samples**: `core/audio/sampler.py` plays real instruments from free libraries (VSCO 2 CE, VCSL, FreePats, Karoryfer, Salamander Grand Piano; list and licences in `core/audio/INSTRUMENTS.md`). Write the score as events `(time, instrument, pitch, duration, velocity, pan)`. Long notes are extended seamlessly, and round-robins avoid the machine-gun effect.
109: - **Plucked and folk strings** (guqin, pipa, shamisen, banjo…): `core/audio/pluck.py`, physical modelling (Karplus–Strong) with bends and vibrato.
110: - **Synthesis** with numpy for chip tunes, drones and effects; no download needed.
111: - **Balance the low end.** Synthetic scores get bass-heavy quickly. Measure energy per band after mixing; keep 20–120 Hz around −3 dB relative to the rest, skip pad notes below MIDI 48, and give the bass some 2nd and 3rd harmonics so it speaks on small speakers.
112: 
113: ## 6. Sound effects and mix
114: 
115: - `core/audio/sfx.py` synthesises foley procedurally (click, whoosh, thump, ding, paper, noise beds…) with filters, envelopes and `add(buffer, sound, at, gain, pan)`. Drive it from `window.EV`, so every sound sits exactly on its frame.
116: - **Master**: `sh core/render/mux.sh video.mp4 mix.wav out.mp4 24 [grain]` muxes, runs a two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS with a true-peak limit, adds grain in ffmpeg and prints the measured loudness; it exits non-zero on any failure. On light backgrounds use less grain; for pixel and vector styles, none.
117: - Films with grain baked into the picture compress badly; re-encode with `-tune grain` and a higher CRF.
118: 
119: ## 7. Subtitles
120: 
121: - Export `.srt` with `core/render/srt.py cues.json out.srt` (cues = `[{t0, t1, text}]`), and burn styled captions into the page itself: the caption design is part of the style.
122: - Timing rules are in DIRECTOR.md §7.
123: 
124: ## 8. Review loop
125: 
126: 1. Contact sheets: a frame every 1–2 s with `still.mjs --range`, tiled with `core/render/sheet.py`. At least two full passes.
127: 2. Frame strips at 0.2 s for every key action: hand-overs, falls, hits.
128: 3. On the final file: `ffmpeg -af ebur128` (loudness), `blackdetect` (blank frames), whisper again on the final mix if it has voice.
129: 4. Watch it once, at full speed, with sound.
130: 
131: ## 9. 3D notes
132: 
133: - three.js r170 rendered headless through WebGL2 on the GPU; physical depth of field and GTAO from `core/three/post.js`, rendered at 2× and downsampled.
134: - Lighting: soft area lights plus a Poly Haven HDRI at low intensity reads more "real" than bright ambient light.
135: - `core/three/post.js` is written for a perspective camera. For an orthographic camera swap `perspectiveDepthToViewZ` for `orthographicDepthToViewZ` in its depth pass, or the depth of field silently breaks.
136: 
137: ## 10. Characters drawn in code
138: 
139: - A 2.5D rig (torso, head, limbs solved per frame) is enough for pantomime.
140: - Order the shoulder rotation as abduction, then flexion; the reverse order crosses raised arms into an X.
141: - Let the shoulder girdle rise and move forward as the arm lifts, and don't outline the part of the arm that overlaps the torso: that line is what makes a joint look like a puppet seam.
142: 
143: ## 11. Assets, credits and fonts
144: 
145: Only CC0, CC BY or OFL material, each listed in the film's `CREDITS` with its source and licence; `core/audio/sampler.py credits(names)` writes the lines for the instruments you used. Public-domain works count as CC0; "no known restrictions" does not. Data or images under other open licences (ODbL, CC BY-SA, open-hardware licences) only after you have named the licence and its terms (attribution, share-alike) to the user and they agree. The user's own material is fine as it is.
146: 
147: A film that states facts (the Evidence Films styles) keeps a `FACTS.md` in the project folder: each claim with its source URL and the quoted wording, or the measurement that produced it.
148: 
149: Fonts: Google Fonts (OFL), self-hosted in the project. The typefaces a `STYLE.md` names are not in the library; download them (`https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/<family>`) into the project's `fonts/`. `core/fonts/` holds a few Latin display fonts and a Chinese display font with only about 200 glyphs, not enough for running Chinese text. For Chinese, subset a CJK font to the characters you use: the Google Fonts CSS API with `&text=` returns just those glyphs (`https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Noto+Sans+SC:wght@700&text=<URL-encoded characters>`). Download the font file it points to into the project's `fonts/` and load it with `@font-face`; don't link Google Fonts at render time.
